advisory.title: Multiple timing variability issues in operations intended to be constant-time
advisory.description:
## Summary

Several operations intended to be constant-time could execute secret-dependent
branches, depending on the compiler and target CPU. These include subtraction,
zero counting, division, and Montgomery multiplication.

Additionally, `UintRef` equality could terminate at the first unequal limb,
and `BoxedMontyForm::invert` branched on whether an inverse exists.

## Impact

Applications using affected operations on secret integers may leak information
through timing or microarchitectural side channels. This includes information
about intermediate arithmetic values, matching limbs, and invertibility.

Such leakage could potentially enable recovery of cryptographic secrets.
Practical exploitability depends on the downstream algorithm, compiler, target
CPU, and an attacker's ability to observe the side channel.

## Resolution

Upgrade to v0.7.6, which removes the identified branches, updates `ctutils` to
include its constant-time fixes, and adds BINSEC-based regression checks using
`cargo checkct` for arithmetic on multiple targets.

advisory.title: Marvin Attack: potential key recovery through timing sidechannels
advisory.description:
### Impact
Due to a non-constant-time implementation, information about the private key is leaked through timing information which is observable over the network. An attacker may be able to use that information to recover the key.

### Patches
No patch is yet available. The crypto-bigint migration ([RustCrypto/RSA#394](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/pull/394)) did not close this. Tracking is [RustCrypto/RSA#626](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/issues/626) (padding still not constant-time). Implicit rejection work is in [RustCrypto/RSA#680](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/pull/680); default-path blinding is in [RustCrypto/RSA#702](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/pull/702).

Still affected as of 2026-09-12: rsa 0.9.10 (latest stable) and rsa 0.10.0-rc.18 (latest). `patched = []` is intentional.

### Workarounds
Avoid using the `rsa` crate in settings where attackers can observe timing, for example over the network. Local use on a non-compromised computer is fine.

### References
This vulnerability was discovered as part of the "[Marvin Attack]", which revealed several implementations of RSA including OpenSSL had not properly mitigated timing sidechannel attacks.

[Marvin Attack]: https://people.redhat.com/~hkario/marvin/

advisory.title: Reachable panic in certificate revocation list parsing
advisory.description:
A panic was reachable when parsing certificate revocation lists via [`BorrowedCertRevocationList::from_der`]
or [`OwnedCertRevocationList::from_der`].  This was the result of mishandling a syntactically valid empty
`BIT STRING` appearing in the `onlySomeReasons` element of a `IssuingDistributionPoint` CRL extension.

This panic is reachable prior to a CRL's signature being verified.

Applications that do not use CRLs are not affected.

Thank you to [@tynus3](https://github.com/tynus3) for the report.

advisory.title: Name constraints for URI names were incorrectly accepted
advisory.description:
Name constraints for URI names were ignored and therefore accepted.

Note this library does not provide an API for asserting URI names, and URI name constraints are otherwise not implemented.  URI name constraints are now rejected unconditionally.

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, this bug is reachable only after signature verification and requires misissuance to exploit.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Name constraints were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name
advisory.description:
Permitted subtree name constraints for DNS names were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name.

This was incorrect because, given a name constraint of `accept.example.com`, `*.example.com` could feasibly allow a name of `reject.example.com` which is outside the constraint.
This is very similar to [CVE-2025-61727](https://go.dev/issue/76442).

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, this bug is reachable only after signature verification and requires misissuance to exploit.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: CRLs not considered authoritative by Distribution Point due to faulty matching logic
advisory.description:
If a certificate had more than one `distributionPoint`, then only the first `distributionPoint` would be considered against each CRL's `IssuingDistributionPoint` `distributionPoint`, and then the certificate's subsequent `distributionPoint`s would be ignored.

The impact was that correctly provided CRLs would not be consulted to check revocation. With `UnknownStatusPolicy::Deny` (the default) this would lead to incorrect but safe `Error::UnknownRevocationStatus`. With `UnknownStatusPolicy::Allow` this would lead to inappropriate acceptance of revoked certificates.

This vulnerability is thought to be of limited impact. This is because both the certificate and CRL are signed -- an attacker would need to compromise a trusted issuing authority to trigger this bug.  An attacker with such capabilities could likely bypass revocation checking through other more impactful means (such as publishing a valid, empty CRL.)

More likely, this bug would be latent in normal use, and an attacker could leverage faulty revocation checking to continue using a revoked credential.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-pwjx-qhcg-rvj4](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-pwjx-qhcg-rvj4). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Certificate verification may accept distrusted intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys when the configured trust anchors allow such paths.
The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

Versions 0.103.16 and 0.104.0-alpha.8 reject paths containing these public keys.

advisory.title: Insecure Preservation of SUID/SGID Bits during ZIP Extraction Leading to Potential Privilege Escalation
advisory.description:
The `zip` crate preserves privileged Unix permission bits (SUID, SGID, and sticky bits) from ZIP `external_attributes` during extraction, instead of masking them to safe permission bits. If a privileged process (for example, `root` in an installer, CI/CD pipeline, or container build) extracts an attacker-controlled ZIP archive using `ZipArchive::extract()` or the stream extraction API, files can be created as setuid-root or setgid. This behavior allows the creation of SUID/SGID files during extraction, which can lead to local privilege escalation depending on the execution environment.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-vv5m-jxxh-4627

advisory.title: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` creates symbolic links whose attacker-controlled targets are outside the destination directory
advisory.description:
In `zip` 9.0.0-pre2, `ZipArchive::extract` creates a symbolic link from an archive entry after validating only the output entry path. The link target bytes are passed directly to the platform symlink API, so a malicious archive can create an entry inside the destination that resolves to an attacker-chosen path outside it. This behavior was verified on macOS and Linux. On either platform, a subsequent application read or write through that extracted entry accesses the external target with the extracting process's permissions.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4v9h-p7m9-rh26

advisory.title: ZipStreamReader::extract() and ZipArchive::extract() apply Unix permissions through symlinks without confining the target
advisory.description:
`ZipStreamReader::extract()` applies Unix permissions through extracted symlinks without validating the symlink target stays within the destination

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4684-h2q9-2vcp

advisory.title: paste - no longer maintained
advisory.description:
The creator of the crate `paste` has stated in the [`README.md`](https://github.com/dtolnay/paste/blob/master/README.md) 
that this project is not longer maintained as well as archived the repository

## Possible Alternative(s)

- [`pastey`]: a fork of paste and is aimed to be a drop-in replacement with additional features for paste crate
- [`with_builtin_macros`]: crate providing a [superset of `paste`'s functionality including general `macro_rules!` eager expansions](https://docs.rs/with_builtin_macros/0.1.0/with_builtin_macros/macro.with_eager_expansions.html)  and `concat!`/`concat_idents!` macros

[`pastey`]: https://crates.io/crates/pastey
[`with_builtin_macros`]: https://crates.io/crates/with_builtin_macros

advisory.title: `ttf-parser` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The author of `ttf-parser` has stated that the crate is unmaintained and will not receive further fixes (see the referenced issue).

## Alternative(s)

- [`skrifa`](https://crates.io/crates/skrifa), an actively maintained TrueType and OpenType font parsing crate, part of the Google Fonts "oxidize" (`fontations`) project.

advisory.title: `zbus_names` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zbus_names` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `names` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus name types.

advisory.title: `zvariant` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zvariant` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `wire` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format. Users of the GVariant format should migrate to [`zgvariant`](https://crates.io/crates/zgvariant).

advisory.title: `zvariant_derive` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zvariant_derive` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

Its derive macros are provided by [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format.

advisory.title: `AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate I/O safety
advisory.description:
`tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd` provides safe constructors (`new`, `with_interest`, `try_new`, and `try_with_interest`) that accept any `T: AsRawFd` rather than requiring proof of ownership or validity of the file descriptor. Because `RawFd` implements `AsRawFd`, safe code can construct an `AsyncFd` from an arbitrary or closed file descriptor, or close/replace the underlying file descriptor while the `AsyncFd` is still alive.

This violates I/O safety in two ways:

1. `AsyncFd<T>` implements `AsFd` for all `T: AsRawFd` by calling `BorrowedFd::borrow_raw(self.as_raw_fd())`, allowing safe code to obtain an arbitrary `BorrowedFd<'_>` without owning the file descriptor.
2. Tokio's I/O driver stores a pointer to an internal allocation in the `epoll`/`kqueue` user data for registered file descriptors. If the underlying file descriptor is duplicated and then closed while an `AsyncFd` is alive, and the OS reuses that file descriptor number for a another IO resource on the same runtime, dropping the first `AsyncFd` deregisters the reused file descriptor number and frees the first while the original file description remains registered in `epoll`, leading to a use-after-free when a readiness event fires.

Starting in Tokio 1.51.6, 1.53.3, and 1.54.0, `AsyncFd::new`, `AsyncFd::with_interest`, `AsyncFd::try_new`, and `AsyncFd::try_with_interest` are deprecated in favor of the `unsafe` constructors `AsyncFd::register` and `AsyncFd::register_with_interest`. Callers must ensure that the file descriptor remains valid, open, and unchanged for the lifetime of the `AsyncFd`.
